To "give someone the slip" means to escape from someone cleverly and secretly, especially when that person is following you, chasing you, or watching you closely.

The key idea is that your escape catches the other person off guard — they don't even realize you're gone until it's too late. You didn't fight them. You didn't confront them. You simply vanished from their attention, smoothly and quietly.

Think of it like a fish slipping out of someone's hand the moment they thought they had caught it. That's the feeling this idiom captures.

The word "slip" is the heart of this idiom. In everyday English, "slip" means to move smoothly, quietly, and without drawing attention — like slipping out of a room while everyone is busy talking. It also carries the sense of something escaping a grip — like soap slipping out of your hands.

So "giving someone the slip" is about making yourself slip away from the person who is trying to keep track of you.

This idiom is believed to have come from two possible sources, both rooted in old, practical life:

1. Hunting with dogs:
In old-fashioned hunting, dogs were kept on leashes called "slips." When hunters wanted to release a dog to chase an animal, they would "give the slip" — meaning they let the leash go so the dog could run free. Over time, the phrase flipped in meaning: instead of releasing something, it came to describe something escaping from you.

2. Sailors and ships:
When a ship was anchored and needed to escape quickly — perhaps from an enemy — the sailors would cut or release the anchor cable instead of slowly pulling it up. This was called "slipping the anchor." The ship would then glide away before anyone could stop it. This sneaky, fast getaway gave us a similar sense of the idiom.

Both origins point to the same core idea: a quick, smooth, unexpected escape.

The idiom has been used in the English language since at least the 16th century, and it remains alive and well in modern English today.

The structure of this idiom is simple:

give + [person] + the slip

You always need to mention who you are escaping from. The idiom doesn't work without that person.

Here are some examples:

  • "The burglar gave the police the slip by sneaking through a back alley."
  • "I didn't want to talk to my boss at the party, so I gave him the slip and left early."
  • "The spy gave her pursuers the slip by blending into the crowd."
  • "The celebrity gave the photographers the slip by leaving through a side exit."
  • "He almost caught me, but I managed to give him the slip."

Notice that in all of these examples, the escape is quiet, sneaky, and unexpected — not a dramatic fight or a loud confrontation.
The Tone and Feel of This Idiom

This is an informal idiom. You would use it in casual conversation, storytelling, or fiction — not in formal writing like a business report or academic essay.

It has a slightly playful or adventurous tone, which is why you'll find it very often in:

  • Crime novels and detective stories
  • Spy thrillers
  • Action movies and TV shows
  • Everyday conversation when telling a fun story
What Makes It Different from Simply "Escaping"

You might wonder: why not just say "escaped from someone"? The idiom adds something that plain words don't. When you say "give someone the slip," you automatically communicate:

  • The escape was sneaky, not forceful
  • The other person was outsmarted or left confused
  • There is a certain cleverness or skill involved
  • The person who escaped had to think quickly or act smartly

Simply saying "I escaped" doesn't carry any of that. The idiom paints a much richer picture in just four words.

The idiom is most often used in the past tense, because you're usually describing something that already happened:

  • "She gave me the slip." ✅ (most common)
  • "He gives everyone the slip." ✅ (present, for habitual behavior)
  • "I'm trying to give them the slip." ✅ (present continuous, in the middle of escaping)

You might also sometimes hear:

  • "Slip away" — a related phrase meaning to leave quietly and unnoticed, though it doesn't need a pursuer: "She slipped away from the party before midnight."
  • "Shake someone off" — similar meaning, but suggests more effort in getting rid of someone following you.
  • "Lose someone" — informal, means to successfully escape a follower: "I think we lost them!"

If you ever forget what this idiom means, picture this scene:

A spy is being followed through a busy market. The moment the enemy blinks, the spy ducks into a doorway, pulls on a hat, and disappears into the crowd. By the time the enemy looks back, the spy is gone — as if they simply slipped right through their fingers.

That image — smooth, clever, silent escape — is exactly what "give someone the slip" means.
